prompt: A middle aged female presents with chronic pain in right side of abdomen with intermittent fever. Clinical examination revealed mild hepatomegaly and hence a contrast enhanced CT abdomen was performed.

sentences.s: Okay, so we have a middle-aged woman who's been dealing with this nagging pain on her right side of the abdomen.
That's not something you can just brush off.
She also has these bouts of fever that come and go.
Hmm, that sounds like there might be some inflammation or infection going on.
Now, when they checked her out, they found she has an enlarged liver.
That's interesting because it makes me think about what could be causing both the liver to swell and the abdominal pain.
It's like two clues pointing towards something happening in the liver area.
So, let's consider what could cause both of these symptoms together.
Liver infections are one possibility.
Hepatitis comes to mind, but usually, hepatitis is more widespread and doesn't just cause localized pain.
Plus, it often causes jaundice too, which isn't mentioned here.
What else?
Ah, pyogenic liver abscesses!
Those can definitely cause localized pain and fever.
They're basically pockets of pus in the liver due to an infection, and they can make the liver swell up.
This seems to fit our patient's situation pretty well.
But wait, let's not jump to conclusions.
What if it's something else?
Could it be a tumor?
Liver cancer, maybe?
But tumors don't usually cause fevers unless they've infected or inflamed nearby tissues.
So, I'm not leaning towards that as much.
Alright, back to the abscess idea.
Pyogenic liver abscesses seem to check all the boxes: localized pain, fever, and hepatomegaly.
Yeah, that feels like the most likely explanation given everything we know.
So, putting it all together, I'd say the most probable diagnosis here is a pyogenic liver abscess.
It just fits the symptoms and findings best.

prompt: A 56-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician because her left breast has become larger, hot, and itchy over the past 2 months. The patient felt a small lump in her left breast 1 year ago but did not seek medical attention at that time. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Menarche was at the age of 11 years and menopause at the age of 46 years. Her mother died of breast cancer at the age of 45 years. The patient does not smoke or drink alcohol. Current medications include labetalol, simvastatin, and daily low-dose aspirin. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 78 kg (172 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.7В°C (99.9В°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Examination shows large dense breasts. There is widespread erythema and edematous skin plaques over a breast mass in the left breast. The left breast is tender to touch and left-sided axillary lymphadenopathy is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, let's think about this.
We've got a 56-year-old woman who's come in with some pretty concerning symptoms in her left breast.
It's gotten bigger, feels hot and itchy, and there's a lump she noticed last year that she didn't follow up on.
That's definitely something we need to pay attention to.
She's got a history of hypertension and high cholesterol, which are both risk factors for cardiovascular issues, but they can also be linked to other conditions.
And then there's her family history—her mom passed away from breast cancer at just 45.
That's really young, so that's a big red flag right there.
Now, she doesn't smoke or drink, which is good, but she's taking labetalol, simvastatin, and aspirin.
Those meds are for her hypertension and cholesterol, but I wonder if they could have any role here.
Maybe not directly, but they're worth keeping in mind.
Her physical exam shows large, dense breasts, which makes me think about how tricky it might be to see what's going on inside them.
But there's more—there's widespread redness and swelling on the skin of her left breast, and it's tender when touched.
Plus, there's lymph node involvement in the armpit on the same side as the problem breast.
That's usually a sign that something's going on locally, maybe an infection or inflammation, or even cancer.
So, what could this all mean?
Inflammatory breast cancer jumps out as a possibility.
It's rare, but it fits with the red, swollen, and tender description.
And the fact that she had a lump before that she ignored adds another layer.
Could it be inflammatory breast cancer?
It seems like it matches up with the symptoms and her family history too.
But wait, let's not jump to conclusions.
Mastitis could cause similar symptoms, especially with the tenderness and swelling.
But mastitis usually happens in breastfeeding women, and she isn't one of those.
So, that's probably not it.
Could it be fibroadenoma?
They're common benign tumors, but they don't usually cause the skin changes we're seeing here.
And they aren't typically painful either.
Hmm, what about breast abscess?
That could explain the redness and swelling, but it would usually follow an infection, and there's no mention of that here.
Alright, back to inflammatory breast cancer.
It's still the best fit given everything—the redness, the swelling, the lymph nodes, and the family history.
Yeah, I'm leaning towards that being the most likely diagnosis.

prompt: A 10 year old male child presents with pallor and h/o blood transfusion 2 months back. On investigation, Hb-4.5 gms, Total count-60,000,Platelet count-2 lakhs and CD 10+ve, CD 19+ve, CD 117 +ve, MPO +ve and CD 33 -ve.

sentences.s: Alright, let's see what we've got here.
We have a 10-year-old boy who is looking pale and has had a blood transfusion just two months ago.
That's definitely concerning because it suggests he might be dealing with some kind of chronic issue that's causing anemia.
Now, let's look at his lab results.
His hemoglobin level is really low at 4.5 g/dL, which confirms the anemia suspicion.
But there's more to consider.
His white blood cell count is through the roof at 60,000, and his platelets are also elevated at 200,000.
This combination of high white cells and platelets makes me think about conditions where the bone marrow is overactive or producing too many cells.
Next up, we have these immunophenotyping markers.
He's positive for CD10, CD19, and CD117, but negative for CD33 and myeloperoxidase (MPO).
Let's break this down.
CD10 and CD19 are typically found on B-cells, so they're hinting towards something related to lymphocytes.
CD117 is interesting because it's usually seen in stem cells and some leukemias, like CML.
But wait, CD33 is a marker for myeloid cells, and he's negative for that, so it doesn't fit with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
So, if we're not looking at AML, what could this be?
The combination of pancytosis—low red cells, high white cells, and high platelets—is making me think of a myeloproliferative disorder.
And with those specific markers, I'm leaning towards a type of leukemia that involves both myeloid and lymphoid lineages.
Given all this, I'm thinking about mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL), specifically the B-lineage type.
It fits because MPAL can show a mix of myeloid and lymphoid features, and the markers match up with that possibility.
So, yeah, based on everything, MPAL seems like the most likely diagnosis here.

prompt: A 17-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The patient was an unrestrained driver in a head-on collision. He has a past medical history of asthma, depression, and anxiety. He is not currently taking any medications. His temperature is 99.5В°F (37.5В°C), blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 115/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. The patient's cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. The patient is breathing on his own and has strong distal pulses. Ultimately, the patient is discharged with follow up instructions after no significant fractures or injuries are found. The patient then presents 4 months later to his primary doctor with weakness. The patient's strength in his upper extremities is 1/5. He has reduced sensation in his upper extremities as well. The patient's lower extremities reveal 5/5 strength with intact sensation. A chest radiograph and basic labs are ordered. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, so we have this 17-year-old guy who just had a car crash.
That's pretty serious, especially since he wasn't wearing a seatbelt.
Let's think about what could happen here.
In these kinds of accidents, there's always a risk of neck or back injuries because those areas can take quite a hit during a head-on collision.
Now, he's got some health issues like asthma, depression, and anxiety.
Those are important to keep in mind because they might affect how he recovers from something like this.
But right now, let's focus on the immediate aftermath of the crash.
No broken bones were found, which is good, but that doesn't rule out everything.
We should still consider soft tissue injuries or even something neurological.
Fast forward four months,
and he's back with his doctor complaining of weakness in his arms.
Hmm, that's concerning.
Weakness in one part of the body without injury in another area makes me think it's probably related to the accident.
It's been a while, so maybe it's something that develops over time, like a chronic issue.
The fact that his arms are weak but his legs are fine suggests something specific.
If it were a general condition, I'd expect both sides of the body to be affected equally.
So, it's more localized, which points towards nerve damage or something similar.
Let's think about what kind of injury could cause this.
Whiplash comes to mind because it's common in car crashes and can lead to neck problems.
These neck issues can mess with nerves, causing weakness and sensory changes in the arms.
Yeah, that seems plausible.
But wait, there's also the possibility of a brachial plexus injury.
This happens when the nerves around the shoulder and neck get damaged, often due to trauma.
It would explain the arm weakness and sensory loss perfectly.
And given the timing, it fits too.
Symptoms like these can develop weeks or months after the initial injury.
So, putting it all together, I'm leaning towards a brachial plexus injury.
It matches the symptoms and the timeline.
Plus, it's consistent with what we know about how these types of injuries can present.
Yeah, that feels like the most likely explanation.

prompt: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of difficulty breathing for the past hour. The parents report noisy breathing and bluish discoloration of their son's lips. During the past two months, the patient has had several upper respiratory tract infections and poor weight gain. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 20th percentile for length and 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38В°C (100.4В°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 80/55 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over both lung fields. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Intubation is performed and methylprednisolone is administered. Methenamine silver staining of bronchial lavage fluid shows aggregates of 2 to 8 cysts with central spores. Serum IgA titers are decreased. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

sentences.s: Okay, so we have a little baby who's having trouble breathing and looks blue around the mouth.
That's definitely concerning.
Let's think about what could be going on here.
The baby's been having these respiratory issues for a while now, like over the last couple of months.
And he's not gaining weight well either.
Poor thing.
This isn't just a one-off thing; it sounds like something chronic or recurring.
Now, let's look at the chest X-ray.
It shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
Hmm, that suggests some kind of infection in the lungs.
But what kind?
We need more clues.
Oh, there's also the lab result showing decreased serum IgA levels.
That's interesting.
Low IgA can mean the immune system isn't working quite right, which might make him more prone to certain infections.
And then there's the methenamine silver stain.
It reveals aggregates of 2 to 8 cysts with central spores in the bronchial lavage fluid.
Wait a minute, that's pretty specific.
Pneumocystis jirovecii comes to mind because it's known for causing similar findings.
But wait, let's not jump to conclusions too quickly.
Pneumocystis usually causes pneumonia in people with weakened immune systems, like those with HIV/AIDS.
Is our little guy immunocompromised?
There's no mention of any serious immune problems here, just low IgA.
So maybe not Pneumocystis after all.
Let's think about other possibilities.
Could it be something like congenital CMV?
That can cause respiratory issues in newborns and sometimes leads to low IgA levels.
Yeah, that fits.

Congenital CMV could explain the recurrent respiratory infections and the low IgA.

So, putting it all together, I'm thinking congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) seems like the most likely explanation.
It matches the symptoms, the lab results, and the lack of an obvious immune deficiency.
Yep, that makes sense.

prompt: A 24-year-old woman with a past medical history of anorexia nervosa presents to the clinic due to heavy menses, bleeding gums, and easy bruisability. She says she is trying to lose weight by restricting her food intake. She has taken multiple courses of antibiotics for recurrent sinusitis over the past month. No other past medical history or current medications. She is not sexually active. Her vital signs are as follows: temperature 37.0В°C (98.6В°F), blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min, respiratory rate 16/min. Her BMI is 16 kg/m2. Her physical examination is significant for ecchymosis on the extremities, dry mucous membranes, and bleeding gums. A gynecological exam is non-contributory. Laboratory tests show a prolonged PT, normal PTT, and normal bleeding time. CBC shows microcytic anemia, normal platelets, and normal WBC. Her urine pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely cause of her condition?

sentences.s: Okay, let's see what's going on here.
We've got a young woman who's dealing with some pretty concerning symptoms.
She's experiencing heavy periods, bleeding gums, and easy bruising.
That's definitely something that makes me think about bleeding disorders right off the bat.
Now, she also has a history of anorexia nervosa.
Hmm, that's interesting because I know that eating disorders can really mess with nutrient levels in the body.
Anorexia can lead to deficiencies in certain vitamins, especially vitamin K, which is important for clotting.
So, maybe that's why she's having these bleeding issues.
Oh, and she's been on antibiotics recently for sinusitis.
Antibiotics can sometimes wipe out good bacteria in the gut, which might affect how well our bodies absorb nutrients.
This could be another reason why she's experiencing these symptoms.
Her lab results show a prolonged PT but normal PTT and bleeding time.
That's a big clue!
It suggests that there's a problem with the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade.

Vitamin K deficiency would fit this picture perfectly since it affects the production of certain clotting factors that rely on vitamin K.

She's also got microcytic anemia.
Microcytic anemia often points towards iron deficiency, which is common in people with anorexia nervosa.
But wait, it could also happen if someone isn't getting enough vitamin C, which is another nutrient that's important for collagen synthesis and wound healing.
So, putting all of this together, we have a combination of bleeding problems, a history of anorexia nervosa, recent antibiotic use, and microcytic anemia.
All of these things seem to point towards a deficiency in either vitamin K or vitamin C. Given the specific lab findings, vitamin K deficiency seems like the more likely culprit.
But wait, let's consider vitamin C again.
Bleeding gums and easy bruising could also be linked to low vitamin C levels.

And if she's not eating well, she might not be getting enough fruits and veggies, which are rich in vitamin C.

Hmm, so while vitamin K deficiency explains the prolonged PT, vitamin C deficiency could explain the gum bleeding and bruising.
Maybe it's both?
Or perhaps one is causing the other.
It's possible that the vitamin C deficiency is making her more prone to bleeding, which then leads to a secondary vitamin K deficiency.
Alright, after thinking through all of this, I'm leaning towards a vitamin C deficiency as the main issue.
The combination of symptoms and her dietary habits make it seem like she's not getting enough vitamin C, leading to poor collagen synthesis and increased bleeding tendency.
Yeah, that feels like the most comprehensive explanation given everything we've got here.

prompt: A 45-year old man presents with a daily headache. He describes two attacks per day over the past 3 weeks. Each attack lasts about an hour and awakens the patient from sleep. The patient has noted associated tearing and reddening of his right eye as well as nasal stuffiness. The pain is deep, excruciating, and limited to the right side of the head. The neurologic examination is nonfocal.

sentences.s: Okay, so we have a 45-year-old guy who's been having these headaches that happen twice a day for the last three weeks.
That's quite frequent!
And they wake him up from sleep?
That's interesting because it suggests something that's really disrupting his rest.
Now, let's think about what else he's experiencing during these headaches.
There's tearing in one eye, redness, and nasal stuffiness on the same side as the headache.
Hmm, this combination of symptoms makes me wonder if there's some kind of nerve involvement here.
It sounds like the trigeminal nerve might be involved since it's responsible for sensation in the face and can cause autonomic symptoms like tearing and nasal congestion when activated.
The fact that the pain is on just one side of the head and is described as deep and excruciating also points towards something specific.
It's not just any headache; it's localized and intense.
This could mean we're dealing with something like migraines or cluster headaches, which are known for being severe and unilateral.
Let's consider the duration too.
These headaches last about an hour each time.
That's pretty short compared to other types of headaches.
Cluster headaches usually come in clusters and are shorter, often lasting between 15 minutes to 3 hours.
So, this fits with that pattern.
Also, the frequency—two times a day—is another clue.
Cluster headaches tend to occur multiple times a day during their active phase.
This matches our patient's experience perfectly.
So, putting all these pieces together—the location, the intensity, the autonomic symptoms, the duration, and the frequency—it seems like we're looking at cluster headaches.
Yeah, that's got to be it.
Everything lines up with how cluster headaches typically present themselves.

prompt: A farmer from central Asia presents with an acute onset of swinging pyrexia, rigor, sweating and monoarticular arthritis of the hip. He also complained of headache and insomnia. On examination he is found to have a small, firm splenom egaly and hepatomegaly. His counts showed leucopenia with relative lypmhocytosis.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see what we've got here.
We've got a farmer from central Asia who suddenly comes down with a fever that swings back and forth, along with chills and night sweats.
That sounds pretty serious.
And there's joint pain too, specifically in one hip.
Hmm, that's interesting.
Joint pain can be a clue pointing towards something specific.
Now, he's also having headaches and trouble sleeping.
Those symptoms could mean a lot of things, but they often show up when the body is fighting off some kind of infection or inflammation.
Let me think about this.
When I examine him, his spleen and liver are both enlarged.
That's not normal, right?
Enlarged organs like that usually mean there's something going on inside, maybe an infection or some sort of systemic issue.
His blood tests show low white blood cell count overall, but more lymphocytes than usual.
So, it seems like his immune system is trying to respond, but maybe it's not working quite right.
This combination of leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis makes me think of certain infections.
Let's piece this together.
Fever, joint pain, organ enlargement, and that particular blood profile.
It feels like we're dealing with something infectious.
Brucellosis jumps out at me because it fits so well.
It's common in farmers, especially those in central Asia, where brucella bacteria are around.
Brucellosis causes fevers, joint pains, and can mess with the liver and spleen, causing them to swell.
Plus, it can cause that weird blood pattern with low white cells but more lymphocytes.
Yeah, that all lines up.
So, putting it all together, I'm thinking this guy has brucellosis.
It just fits with everything we know about his symptoms and background.
Makes sense!

prompt: A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found on the floor in front of his apartment. On physical examination, an alcoholic smell and slurred speech are noted. Neurological exam shows diminished deep tendon reflexes bilaterally and an ataxic gait. His pupils are normal. sentences.s: Okay, so we have a 46-year-old guy who was found on the floor outside his apartment.
That's already concerning.
He's not fully awake but can respond when you try to talk to him.
Let's see what else is going on.
His vital signs seem pretty stable—pulse is 64 beats per minute, breathing is 15 breaths per minute, and blood pressure is 120 over 75.
Those numbers look okay, nothing alarming there.
But wait, he smells like alcohol?
And his speech is slurred.
Hmm, that could mean something, especially with the whole being-found-on-the-floor thing.
Now, let's think about his neurological exam.
Diminished deep tendon reflexes and an ataxic gait—that's interesting.
It suggests some kind of nerve or muscle issue.
Slurred speech and ataxia make me wonder if it's related to something affecting coordination or balance.
Oh, and his blood alcohol level is only 0.04%, which is actually quite low.
So, it doesn't explain everything.
I'm thinking there might be more to this than just alcohol.
Let's consider other possibilities.
Could it be a metabolic problem?
Maybe something like hypoglycemia or electrolyte imbalance?
Or maybe a vitamin deficiency?
Thiamine deficiency comes to mind because it can cause confusion and ataxia too.
But wait, thiamine deficiency usually causes Wernicke's encephalopathy, right?
That would fit with the confusion and ataxia.
And it often happens in people who drink a lot.
So, even though his BAC is low, he might still be dealing with withdrawal or some lingering effects from drinking.
So, putting all these pieces together—the confusion, the ataxia, the history of possible heavy drinking—it really seems like Wernicke's encephalopathy is the most likely explanation here.
Yeah, that makes sense.
It's a classic scenario for this condition.

prompt: Kallu, a 22 year old male had an outing with his friends and developed fever of 38.5 degree C, diarrhoea and vomiting following eating chicken salad. 24 hours back. Two of his friends developed the same symptoms.

sentences.s: Okay, let's think about this.
Kallu went out with his friends and then got sick after eating chicken salad.
That's interesting because it makes me wonder if something in that food could be causing his illness.
Now, he has a fever, diarrhea, and vomiting.
These are pretty common symptoms when someone gets food poisoning.
Hmm, what kind of infections can you get from food?
There are several possibilities.
Bacteria like Salmonella or Campylobacter come to mind.
They're known for causing problems after eating undercooked poultry.
And then there's Staphylococcus aureus, which is more about toxins in food, often linked to dairy or meat products.
But wait, Kallu ate chicken, so maybe that's more relevant here.
Oh, and two of his friends also got sick.
That's a big clue!
If they all ate the same thing, it's probably not just a coincidence.
It's more likely that whatever they ate was contaminated.
So, I'm thinking it's some kind of bacterial infection that spreads easily through food.
Let's see, if we consider the timing.
The symptoms started about 24 hours after eating.
That's a key detail.
Some bacteria have incubation periods around that time frame.
For example, Salmonella usually takes between 12 to 72 hours to show up, while Staphylococcus aureus is typically quicker, showing symptoms in 1-6 hours.
Hmm, given the timeline, Salmonella seems more likely.
So, putting it all together, Kallu and his friends got sick after eating chicken salad, and their symptoms match up with a bacterial infection.
Considering the timing and the fact that multiple people are affected, I'd say it's probably Salmonellosis.

prompt: A 52-year-old man was brought to the emergency department at this hospital because of chest pain and ST-segment elevations on electrocardiography (ECG). The patient had been in his usual health, with hypertension, dyslipidemia, and coronary artery disease, until approximately 8:30 on the morning of admission, when his girlfriend found him lying on the floor of his home, unresponsive; she called emergency medical services (EMS). Shortly thereafter, he regained consciousness, rose to sit in a chair, and reported chest pain and dizziness. He took two nitroglycerin tablets (sublingually). On examination by EMS personnel at 8:42 a.m., he was alert and oriented and appeared uncomfortable; he had pale and diaphoretic skin and was grasping at his sternum and moaning. He reported that he had taken his regular daily aspirin (325 mg, orally) earlier. Respirations and pulse were normal; a faint carotid pulse was palpated; jugular venous distention was not visible. In the ambulance, cardiac monitoring revealed a sinus rate of 56 beats per minute, without ectopy. Nausea and vomiting developed. Supplemental oxygen was administered through a nonrebreather face mask at a rate of 15 liters per minute, and intravenous catheters (18 gauge) were inserted into the antecubital vein in the right arm and a vein in the left forearm. At 8:50 a.m., the blood pressure was 110/90 mm Hg, the pulse 51 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 98%, with the patient reporting chest pain rated at 7 on a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 indicating the most severe pain. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 60 beats per minute; ST-segment elevation of 2 to 3 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) and in leads V3through V6and of 2 mm in right-sided leads V4and V5; and ST-segment depression with T-wave inversion in leads aVL, V1, and V2. Transport to this hospital began at 8:52 a.m. Three minutes later, the patient vomited, became increasingly pale and diaphoretic, and was unresponsive to voice. Normal saline (a 500-ml bolus) was administered. An attempt at tracheal intubation was unsuccessful. However, since a gag reflex was present, a nasopharyngeal airway was inserted instead, without complication. Thereafter, the patient was noted to be breathing on his own. The ambulance arrived at the hospital at 9:04 a.m. The patient had a history of coronary artery disease with unstable angina; 12 years before admission, at another hospital, a bare-metal stent (3.0 mm by 24.0 mm) had been placed in the middle portion of the left anterior descending coronary artery at the level of bifurcation with the first diagonal artery. Seven years later, angina recurred, and a nuclear stress test was positive for anterior ischemia; repeat cardiac catheterization at the other hospital revealed obstructing lesions (95% and 60%) in the left circumflex artery, and two drug-eluting stents were placed. Medications the patient was taking before admission were unknown; in the past he had reportedly taken atorvastatin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and aspirin (325 mg) daily. He had reported no allergies. The patient was divorced and lived with his girlfriend, with visits by his children. He worked in the construction and entertainment industries. Family members reported that he drank alcohol in moderation and had stopped smoking 11 years earlier. There was a family history of coronary artery disease. In the emergency department triage area, the patient was alert and oriented; the blood pressure was 110/90 mm Hg, and the pulse 70 beats per minute. Within seconds after he arrived, the pulse decreased to 36 beats per minute and the width of the QRS complexes on the cardiac monitor increased. External pacing was attempted, without mechanical capture. Seizure activity occurred briefly, and runs of ventricular tachycardia with wide ventricular complexes were seen; the blood pressure and carotid pulses could not be obtained, and the patient was unresponsive. The cardiac monitor revealed ventricular fibrillation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was begun, and the patient was moved to a resuscitation bay. The plasma level of total carbon dioxide was 19.5 mmol per liter (reference range, 23.0 to 31.9), the anion gap 17 mmol per liter (reference range, 3 to 15), the level of phosphorus 2.3 mg per deciliter (0.7 mmol per liter; reference range, 2.6 to 4.5 mg per deciliter [0.8 to 1.5 mmol per liter]), and the level of glucose 145 mg per deciliter (8.0 mmol per liter; reference range, 70 to 110 mg per deciliter [3.9 to 6.1 mmol per liter]). Blood levels of other electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, total protein, albumin, and globulin were normal, as were the results of a complete blood count and tests of liver and renal function; screening for troponin I was negative. During resuscitation, the trachea was intubated. Amiodarone and lidocaine were administered intravenously and nine direct-current countershocks were administered. There was no resolution of the ventricular fibrillation. Management decisions were made.

A soft-tissue, pleural-based lesion is shown in the right apex (Panel A, arrow), and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy is present (Panel B, arrow). On an image of the lower chest, a large retroperitoneal mass is visible (Panel C, arrows). CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis were obtained 3 days later (Panels D and E). Extensive contiguous retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy is shown, with attenuation of the renal vasculature, hydronephrosis of the right kidney, and infiltration of the left kidney proximally (Panel D, arrow). The lymphadenopathy extends below the aortic bifurcation and into the small-bowel mesentery (Panel E, arrow). Three days later, the patient was seen by her internist. On examination, the blood pressure was 160/90 mm Hg, the pulse 80 beats per minute, and the body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) 30.8. An enlarged lymph node (1.0 cm in cross-sectional diameter) was detected on palpation under the pectoralis major muscle in the anterior right axilla. The remainder of the examination was normal. Blood levels of iron, iron-binding capacity, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase, and carcinoembryonic antigen were normal, as were the results of renal-function tests. Cytologic examination of the urine revealed reactive transitional cells and neutrophils but no malignant cells. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, performed 3 days after the patient’s presentation to the emergency department, revealed a massive conglomerate of enlarged lymph nodes; it extended from the level of the celiac axis to below the aortic bifurcation and into the pelvis, and it resulted in marked attenuation of the renal vessels and inferior vena cava, hydronephrosis of the right kidney, and infiltration of soft tissue into the left kidney (Figure 1D). The soft-tissue abnormality extended into the small-bowel mesentery (Figure 1E) and along the pelvic sidewalls. The liver and spleen were normal, as were all the other abdominal organs and the bowel. The next day, the patient was seen by a urologist, and 8 days after that, she was seen by a surgeon, who recommended a retroperitoneal biopsy. Two weeks after her initial presentation, she was seen again by her internist. The patient reported intermittent edema of the left leg with mild pain, dyspnea on exertion, moderate discomfort in the left lower abdomen, and night sweats. On examination, enlarged lymph nodes were detected on palpation under the pectoralis muscles bilaterally, and the left thigh and calf were edematous, without tenderness or tension. sentences.s: Okay, let's see what's going on with this patient.

Her vital signs seem stable enough, but her blood pressure is a bit high at 145/95 mm
Hg.

Plus, it's known for causing progressive dyspnea and cough after an infection.
Yeah, that feels like it fits better.
The post-infectious link, the gradual worsening, and the absence of X-ray changes all point towards BOOP.

sentences.s: Okay, so we have a 23-year-old woman who's come in with knee pain.

Hmm, that could definitely put stress on the knee.
Now, let's think about what else is going on.
She's got a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome and is on birth control pills.

Her vital signs seem okay, nothing alarming there.

she's been doing.

prompt: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-year history of headaches, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and bilateral leg weakness. Skull films reveal hyperostosis of the calvarium. Biopsy of the responsible lesion shows a whorling pattern of the cells.

sentences.s: Okay, let's see what we've got here.

She's experiencing headaches, which are never fun, but she also has generalized tonic-clonic seizures and bilateral leg weakness.
That sounds like something neurological is going on.
Now, when I hear about skull issues in adults, my mind immediately jumps to things like tumors or maybe some kind of bone disorder.
So, they did a skull film and found hyperostosis of the calvarium.
Hmm, that means there's abnormal thickening of the skull bones.
This could be due to several conditions, but it's definitely worth noting.
Next up, they took a biopsy of this lesion, and it showed a whorling pattern of cells.
Whorling?
That rings a bell.
It's not just any old cell arrangement; it's specific.
In medical terms, whorling often points towards certain types of lesions, especially those that are benign or slow-growing.
So, let's think about what fits all these clues together.
Headaches, seizures, leg weakness, and a whorling pattern in the biopsy.
These are classic signs of something like meningioma.
Meningiomas are known for causing these kinds of symptoms because they can press on important structures in the brain.
And the whorling pattern is a big clue here since meningiomas often show that under the microscope.
But wait, let's not jump to conclusions too quickly.
There are other possibilities.
Hyperostosis can also occur in Paget's disease, which affects bone growth and might cause similar changes in the skull.
However, Paget's usually doesn't come with seizures unless it causes complications like a fracture or bleeding in the brain.
And the whorling pattern isn't typical for Paget's either.
Let's consider osteosarcoma next.
It's a type of aggressive bone cancer that could cause hyperostosis, but it's rare in adults and would probably present more aggressively than this.
Plus, the whorling pattern isn't really its thing.
Hmm, so back to meningioma.
It seems to fit well with the symptoms and the biopsy findings.
The whorling pattern is a strong indicator, and the way her symptoms have developed over time matches how meningiomas typically progress.
Yeah, I'm feeling confident about this.
Meningioma seems like the most likely diagnosis given everything we know.

prompt: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning causing him to experience several episodes of nausea and vomiting. sentences.s: Okay, so here's what we've got.

Let's think about what could cause something like this.

His vitals look good—temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, breathing, all normal.

And if they're lying flat, it gets better.
That fits perfectly with what's happening here.
So, yeah, based on how quickly everything started and stopped, and how his symptoms get worse when his head is turned to the left, it really sounds like benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
That's where the room-spinning sensation happens due to tiny crystals in the ear moving around.
It's common and matches up with what's going on here.
I'm pretty confident that's what's going on.
Everything lines up with BPPV.

prompt: A 56-year-old man has painful weeping rashes over the upper eyelid and forehead for the last 2 days along with ipsilateral acute punctuate keratopathy. About a year back, he had chemotherapy for Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. There is no other abnormality.

sentences.s: Okay, let's think about this.

Alright, so let's go back to the idea of an infection.

prompt: A 27 year old man in noted to have blood pressure of 170/100 mmHg. prompt: About 12 days after a mild upper respiratory infection, a 12-year-old boy complains of weakness in his lower extremities. Over several days, the weakness progresses to include his trunk. sentences.s: Okay, so we have this 12-year-old kid who's been feeling weak in his legs about two weeks after having a cold-like illness.

Given all these thoughts, I'm leaning towards Guillain-Barré syndrome.
The post-infectious onset, the way the symptoms are progressing, and the CSF profile all fit pretty well.

prompt: A 70-year-old woman was seen in the memory disorders clinic of this hospital because of progressive cognitive difficulties involving word finding. There was no history of recent head injury, stroke, seizure, transient ischemic attack, meningitis, encephalitis, exposure to human immunodeficiency virus, thyroid disorder, heart disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, liver disease, kidney disease, cancer, pulmonary disorders, exposure to heavy metals, or learning disability. Her only surgical history included three cesarean sections. Her medications were a multivitamin, vitamin C, ginkgo biloba, calcium, magnesium, and zinc, and she had no known allergies. Since the death of her husband 10 years earlier, she had lived alone (in a different state than her daughter) and was able to perform all activities of daily living independently, including managing her money, paying bills, and volunteering in the community (i.e., visiting senior centers to play piano and attending regular community choir practices). She drank alcohol once or twice per month and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. She had been a teacher and had later worked in business with her husband until his death. A brother in his 60s had Parkinson’s disease, and a sister in her 80s had Parkinson’s disease and dementia. Her six children and her grandchildren were healthy. On examination, the patient was alert, attentive, well-groomed, cooperative, and pleasant. The blood pressure was 120/70 mm Hg, the pulse 78 beats per minute and regular, and the weight 68.6 kg. She had a score on the Mini–Mental State Examination of 28 (with scores ranging from 0 to 30 and higher scores indicating better cognitive function), because she was unable to recall the name of the hospital or the county. She had a score on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale of 0 (with scores ranging from 0 to 3 and lower scores indicating better cognitive function). The neurologic examination was normal, including evaluation of the 2nd through 12th cranial nerves, power, bulk, tone, coordination, stance, and gait; the deep tendon reflexes were 1+ throughout. The platelet count was 362,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 150,000 to 350,000), and the folate level was 20 ng per milliliter (45 nmol per liter; reference range, 3 to 17 ng per milliliter [7 to 39 nmol per liter]). The hematocrit, hemoglobin level, white-cell count, and blood levels of vitamin B12, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, total protein, albumin, globulin, and thyrotropin were normal, as were the results of renal- and liver-function tests. A rapid plasma reagin test was nonreactive, and testing for antibodies toBorrelia burgdorferiwas negative. As part of the standard evaluation for a suspected cognitive impairment, the patient was referred for neuropsychological testing, speech pathological evaluation, and imaging studies of the head. On neuropsychological testing, the patient’s performance on a screen of nonverbal abilities indicated that she had average premorbid intellectual abilities. Language impairment was evident both through clinical observations and when she performed verbal tasks, including tasks of confrontation naming, verbal fluency (for which she had substantially more difficulty with semantic fluency than with phonemic fluency), verbal abstraction, and comprehension of individual words. Her spontaneous speech was fluent, but she had notable difficulty with word finding and made occasional paraphasic errors. She often had difficulty comprehending words, such as “cork,” “misplaced,” “bored,” and “pessimism.” Her performance on tests of attention and executive functioning varied; her greatest impairments were evident when the tasks required language mediation, and these impairments contrasted with her generally normal performance on tasks that were not verbally mediated. Similarly, her performance was normal on a test of nonverbal memory but was substantially impaired on a test of verbal memory. Her storage of verbal information was difficult to assess because of her impaired acquisition and anomia. Her storage of nonverbal information was normal, as was her performance on visuospatial tasks. She did not report symptoms of depression or anxiety on self-reported assessments. Ms. Daisy Hochberg:Speech pathological evaluation revealed that the patient had fluent, articulate speech with pauses for word finding, vague word substitutions, and circumlocutions. She was somewhat tangential in her speech and was fixated on telling stories from her life, such that she required frequent refocusing on the topic at hand. She had substantial impairment on a test of naming, with superordinate responses, and she had impairment on word–picture matching. Rare phonemic paraphasias were present. Auditory comprehension was impaired for words she no longer recognized and for sentences with complex syntax. Sentence repetition was intact. A written language assessment revealed that she could read normally and had mild agrammatism in written language samples. A semantic picture–picture matching test revealed no evidence of visual agnosia. (A portion of the speech pathological evaluation is shown inVideo 1, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.) A clinical diagnosis was made, and additional diagnostic tests were performed.

prompt: A 21-year-old woman was evaluated at this hospital because of fatigue, weight gain, and abdominal pain. The patient had been well until 4 months before the current evaluation, when an episode of dull, aching pain in the right lower quadrant occurred. The pain lasted for a few hours before resolving spontaneously. During the next 4 months, episodes of abdominal pain continued to occur and increased in duration, frequency, and severity. The patient sought evaluation in the gynecology clinic of this hospital. On evaluation, the patient described the pain as variable, rating it between 3 and 8 on a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 indicating the most severe pain. The episodes of pain occurred daily and lasted for up to 20 hours. The pain decreased with sitting or lying down and did not increase with movement; it was not associated with her menstrual period. The patient also reported fatigue, irritability, and weight gain of 4.5 kg in the previous 4 months despite increased exercise and decreased food intake. There was a history of hypothyroidism, anxiety, irritable bowel syndrome, and migraines. The patient had never been pregnant and had no known history of sexually transmitted infections or abnormal results on screening tests for cervical cancer. She had previously been sexually active with male partners, but she reported no current sexual activity. She had taken oral contraceptives for 2 years but had stopped taking them 6 months before this evaluation, when a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) was placed. Other medications included levothyroxine, citalopram, and multivitamins; there were no known drug allergies. The patient lived with roommates in an urban area of New England. She was a former athlete and worked as a research scientist. She did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. Her family history included hypothyroidism in her mother, coronary artery disease and hyperlipidemia in her father, breast cancer and diabetes in her paternal grandmother, and lung cancer in her paternal grandfather. On examination, the blood pressure was 119/73 mm Hg and the heart rate 62 beats per minute. The body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) was 28.4. The thyroid was firm on palpation, with a small nodule noted on the right side. The abdomen was nondistended, soft, and nontender. A small hernia with a thrill was noted at the right inguinal ring. A speculum examination of the vagina and cervix was normal; IUD strings were visible at the cervical os. The complete blood count was normal, as were blood levels of electrolytes and glucose and results of tests for kidney, liver, and thyroid function. Screening tests for gonorrhea, chlamydia, human immunodeficiency virus, and syphilis were negative. Imaging studies were obtained. Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mass (measuring 4.8 cm by 5.0 cm by 3.9 cm) along the posterior aspect of the right hepatic lobe (Figure 1A). The uterus, ovaries, and adnexa were normal. There was no free fluid in the pelvis, and the IUD was in an appropriate position. Imaging Studies.A sagittal ultrasound image (Panel A) shows a hypoechoic mass (arrow) posterior to the right lobe of the liver. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a mass arising from the right adrenal gland that is isointense on a T2-weighted image (Panel B, arrow) and has diffusion restriction on a diffusion-weighted image (Panel C, arrow). Computed tomographic images obtained before the administration of contrast material (Panel D), during the portal-venous phase (Panel E), and during the 15-minute delayed phase (Panel F) show the density of the mass (arrows and dashed circles); the absolute washout is 71%. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen, performed before and after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed a right adrenal mass (measuring 4.5 cm by 4.7 cm by 4.0 cm) that was T2 isointense (Figure 1B) and T1 hypointense. The mass had diffusion restriction (Figure 1C), as well as early enhancement with washout, which refers to the temporal reduction in the enhancement of a lesion. The features were indeterminate and were not definitively diagnostic of adrenal adenoma or another adrenal lesion, such as pheochromocytoma or adrenocortical carcinoma. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis again revealed a right adrenal mass, which had a density of 33 Hounsfield units (HU) before the administration of contrast material (Figure 1D), 74 HU during the portal-venous phase (Figure 1E), and 45 HU during the 15-minute delayed phase (Figure 1F). The absolute washout was calculated as 71%. The absolute washout is calculated by dividing the difference between the portal-venous–phase density and the delayed-phase density by the difference between the portal-venous–phase density and the unenhanced density and then converting the result to a percentage: [(HU portal-venous phase − HU delayed phase) / (HU portal-venous phase − HU unenhanced)] × 100. Adrenal adenomas tend to wash out faster than other adrenal lesions, and an absolute washout of more than 60% is highly suggestive of an adrenal adenoma. However, lesions larger than 4 cm are likely to be malignant, regardless of the washout characteristics.1There was also a thin-walled cyst (measuring 3.3 cm in diameter) in the lower lobe of the left lung. The patient was referred to the endocrinology clinic of this hospital. Additional laboratory tests were performed to further evaluate the adrenal mass. Blood levels of renin and aldosterone were normal, as were urinary levels of catecholamines and metanephrines. An overnight, low-dose dexamethasone suppression test was performed. The baseline blood corticotropin level was 3 pg per milliliter (0.7 pmol per liter; reference range, 6 to 76 pg per milliliter [1.3 to 16.7 pmol per liter]). At 11 p.m., dexamethasone (1 mg) was administered; at 8 a.m., the blood cortisol level was 9.1 μg per deciliter (251 nmol per liter; reference value, <1.8 μg per deciliter [50 nmol per liter]), and the concurrent blood dexamethasone level was 631 ng per deciliter (reference range, 140 to 295). The 24-hour urinary free cortisol level was 31.0 μg (reference range, 3.5 to 45.0); the blood levels of dehydroepiandrosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate were normal. Management decisions were made.

Now, what's interesting is that his JVP, or jugular venous pressure, is only 4 cm.

And his heart sounds are normal too, so no murmurs or gallops that might suggest heart problems.

Normally, when you have low sodium, the body tries to conserve it by keeping less in the urine.
But here, the opposite is happening, suggesting that the kidneys are losing sodium.
So, putting all this together, we've got a lung mass, low sodium, normal JVP, and the kidneys aren't holding onto sodium.
This combination makes me think of SIADH, where the body produces too much antidiuretic hormone, causing water retention and diluting the sodium in the blood.
It's like the body is holding onto water instead of salt, leading to low sodium levels.
Also, the fact that he has a lung mass could mean there's a tumor producing ADH, which is a common scenario in SIADH.

prompt: A 48-year-old man was seen in the emergency department of this hospital because of confusion. They were then unable to reach him by telephone for 72 hours and became increasingly concerned about his well-being. Ultimately, he was reached by telephone; he was agitated and refused to board his scheduled return flight. The patient’s mother traveled from the United States to Mexico, where she found the patient to be confused and unkempt and to have lost his wallet and passport; he was drinking alcohol and insisting that he needed to travel immediately to New York City to work on an important legal case. He was single, lived alone in an urban area of New England, and frequently traveled to Mexico; he had sex with men and used condoms intermittently. He drank alcohol in moderation and did not smoke or use illicit drugs. There was no family history of dementia, stroke, seizure disorder, cancer, depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia. On examination, the patient appeared thin and agitated. The temperature was 35.8°C, the pulse 71 beats per minute, the blood pressure 120/62 mm Hg, the respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 99% while he was breathing ambient air. He was alert and oriented to which city he was in and to the year but not the month. When he was asked why he was in the emergency department, his response revealed anosognosia and confabulation. He had nonfluent aphasia and perseverated when speaking, but he had no dysarthria and was able to repeat words, name objects and the current president, and pantomime brushing his hair and teeth. He performed simple calculations accurately but was unable to perform two-part commands; he was slow when he spelled “table” and “world” backward and when he counted down from 100 in increments of 7. He could not provide abstract explanations for proverbs. Examination of the function of cranial nerves II through XII revealed left-eye ptosis, a finding that was also visible on the patient’s driver’s license photograph, which had been taken in the remote past. There was intermittent twitching on the right side of the face. Pronator drift was present on the right side of the body; the motor examination was otherwise normal, as were examinations of sensation and deep-tendon reflexes. Finger–nose–finger movements were smooth and accurate bilaterally after the patient understood the task. The stance and stride were normal, but the patient walked slowly and was unable to walk with a tandem gait or on his toes or heels. The Romberg test was negative. Examination of the skin revealed a purple-brown scaly papule (0.5 cm in diameter) on the medial left knee (Figure 1A), a nonblanching purple-brown patch (1.5 cm in diameter) on the medial aspect of the left palmar foot (Figure 1B), and purple macules on the hard and soft palates. There were also multiple erythematous scars, including one on the left arm with an area of hard scale at the periphery; a red plaque (3 cm in diameter) on the chest with heaped-up central scale, hemorrhagic crust, and purulent discharge; a red plaque (4 cm in diameter) on the left flank with focal areas of scale and brown crust; gritty papules on the face; a large scaly red plaque on the back; and flaky scale on the scalp. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. The red-cell indexes, anion gap, and results of renal-function tests were normal, as were blood levels of calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, vitamin B12, and thyrotropin. Urinalysis showed 1+ leukocyte esterase, 1+ bacteria, a pH of 6.0, and a specific gravity of 1.014; there were 3 to 5 red cells and 10 to 20 white cells per high-power field. Urine and blood toxicology screens were negative. Other laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. Clinical Photographs of Skin Lesions.Panel A shows a purple-brown scaly papule (0.5 cm in diameter) on the medial left knee, and Panel B shows a nonblanching purple-brown patch (1.5 cm in diameter) on the medial aspect of the left palmar foot. Photographs courtesy of Computed tomography of the head revealed ill-defined hypodensities in the white matter of the frontal lobes, which extended into the genu of the corpus callosum, and in the posterior periventricular white matter (Figure 2A). There was also an extraaxial calcification (4 cm in diameter) overlying the right frontal lobe that was thought to possibly represent a partially calcified meningioma (Figure 2B). CT Scan of the Head.An axial image obtained at the level of the lateral ventricles shows abnormal hypodensities that involve the subcortical and deep white matter and most prominently involve the frontal lobes (Panel A). A coronal image shows an extraaxial calcified mass adjacent to the right frontal lobe that most likely represents a calcified meningioma (Panel B, arrow). Six hours after the patient arrived in the emergency department, he had a 2-minute episode of aphasia. The temperature was 38.2°C. Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, acyclovir, and levetiracetam were administered intravenously, and additional imaging studies were obtained. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was performed with and without the administration of intravenous contrast material (Figure 3). T2-weighted images showed an abnormal hyperintense signal in the frontoparietal white matter that was slightly more prominent in the right frontal lobe than in the left frontal lobe and that extended into the genu of the corpus callosum; there was no local mass effect or abnormal restricted diffusion. There was also a small exophytic hypointense lesion along the inner table of the right frontal bone that was suggestive of a small calcified meningioma, as well as mild bilateral prominence of the parotid glands, which had restricted diffusion. MRI of the Head.An axial fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image obtained at the level of the lateral ventricles shows abnormal increased signal in the subcortical and deep white matter that predominantly involves the frontal lobes (Panel A). These abnormalities correspond to those seen on the CT scan. An axial, contrast-enhanced, T1-weighted image obtained at the level of the lateral ventricles shows no abnormal contrast enhancement (Panel B). After the MRI, the patient had another 2-minute witnessed episode, during which he was staring, twitching, and unable to speak; afterward, he seemed to be more confused than he had been previously. A lumbar puncture was performed. The opening pressure was 9 cm of water, and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear and colorless, without xanthochromia. Examination of the CSF revealed 4 red cells and 7 white cells per microliter, a white-cell differential count of 80% lymphocytes and 20% monocytes, a protein level of 97 mg per deciliter (reference range, 5 to 55), and a glucose level of 53 mg per deciliter (2.9 mmol per liter [reference range, 50 to 75 mg per deciliter; 2.8 to 4.2 mmol per liter]). true_dx: Advanced acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) complicated by human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) encephalopathy. Basal-cell carcinoma. Kaposi’s sarcoma.

prompt: A boy who was 14 years 8 months of age and had multiple chronic illnesses was seen in the gastroenterology clinic of this hospital because he had had abnormal results on liver-function tests for approximately 1.5 years. At 2 years of age, he underwent genetic evaluation at another hospital, and the chromosomes were reportedly normal. When the patient was 10 years of age, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head (Figure 1A) was performed because of chronic headaches and nausea. The images showed numerous nonspecific, nonenhancing lesions (measuring ≤8 mm in diameter) in the bilateral periventricular and corona radiata white matter. Results of magnetic resonance angiography were normal. Imaging Studies.An MRI study was performed when the patient was 10 years of age. An axial, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image (Panel A) shows numerous nonspecific focal lesions (measuring ≤8 mm in diameter) throughout the periventricular and corona radiata white matter (arrow); the lesions did not show enhancement after the administration of intravenous gadolinium. These findings are nonspecific and can be caused by myelination disorders, vasculitis, and certain infections, such as Lyme disease. Further imaging studies were performed when the patient initially presented to the gastroenterology clinic, at 14 years of age. A sagittal ultrasound image of the right hepatic lobe (Panel B) shows heterogeneously hypoechoic parenchymal nodules (measuring ≤1 cm in diameter) (arrows) but no dominant mass; the appearance is reminiscent of macronodular cirrhosis. A monospot test was negative, as was testing for Lyme disease and DNA for CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy). When the patient was 13 years of age, laboratory testing revealed normal blood levels of total protein and albumin; other test results are shown inTable 1. Between 13 years 6 months of age and 14 years 6 months of age, the patient’s prothrombin-time international normalized ratio, lipid profile, and red-cell osmotic fragility were normal, as were blood levels of ceruloplasmin, iron, iron-binding capacity, IgG, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) and the 24-hour urinary copper level. Medications included insulin (by pump) and levothyroxine. He had no known allergies to medications. He attended special-education classes in high school and lived with his parents and siblings. His mother and father were both of Italian and Irish ancestry. A maternal uncle had been born prematurely and had a history of learning disabilities, developmental delay, hypogammaglobulinemia (that required infusions of intravenous immune globulin), cryptogenic cirrhosis (that had been diagnosed when he was 30 years of age and was complicated by the hepatopulmonary syndrome), splenic-artery aneurysms, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and bone marrow failure; he died in his 40s.
